strengths: The paper targets an important and timely problem: evaluating LLM-driven GUI agents on long-horizon, cross-platform tasks while avoiding ambiguous final-state judging and costly manual evaluation.

NaturalGAIA’s Causal Pathway design is compelling. Atomic, deterministically verifiable steps and the “Path Collapse” signal provide process-level supervision, localize failures, and make long-horizon evaluation more rigorous than purely outcome-based benchmarks.

The multi-level evaluation framework is useful. WPSR captures difficulty-weighted success, MATCR measures reliable prefix completion, p-ATSR emphasizes later-stage coherence, and the error taxonomy distinguishes planning, structural-compliance, perceptual, knowledge, and operational failures.

The 523 human-verified trajectories are a valuable resource. The structured perception–thought–action–observation–reflection format, inclusion of corrective trajectories, and preservation of diverse interaction strategies should support future GUI-agent training and analysis.

LightManus shows clear empirical gains over PC-Agent and Mobile-Agent-e when using the same Gemini-2.5-Pro backbone: overall Pass@1 rises to 40.0% from 20.0% and 22.9%, while WPSR rises to 29.9% from 14.6% and 23.2%.

The model comparison is broad and the findings are nuanced. Even Claude-sonnet-4 achieves only 34.6% WPSR, and the Qwen2.5-VL-7B results show that T-RFT improves Bearer [REDACTED] but degrades or transfers poorly on the most complex tasks.
The paper is clearly written, and Figure 1 effectively explains the three-stage task parsing, workflow management, and atomic execution architecture.
weaknesses: The baseline comparison is not fully fair for isolating architectural benefit. PC-Agent and Mobile-Agent-e are platform-specific systems, whereas NaturalGAIA explicitly requires cross-platform scheduling. LightManus’s advantage may therefore come substantially from functionality that the baselines lack rather than from better GUI execution alone.

There are no component ablations for the Task Parser, Workflow Manager, Manager, Operator, Reflector, cross-device scheduling, or reflection mechanism. Thus, the central claim that the hierarchical architecture itself causes the improvement is not fully established.

The relationship between the 523 collected trajectories, the 278 training trajectories, the 265 atomic generation tasks, and the 276 benchmark tasks is unclear. The paper needs an explicit task/atomic-step/application split and evidence that evaluation trajectories or solutions were not included in T-RFT training.

Publicly releasing all trajectories could contaminate the benchmark if the corresponding NaturalGAIA tasks remain active. A held-out or hidden evaluation split, timestamped tasks, or contamination controls are needed.

The trajectory data are generated by the proposed LightManus system using Gemini-2.5-Pro and only subsequently filtered by humans. This may encode biases toward LightManus’s planning format and interaction style; independent human demonstrations or trajectories from several agents would strengthen the dataset’s neutrality.

T-RFT is methodologically underspecified. Despite being described as trajectory-reinforced or policy-based fine-tuning, the main text does not clearly define the reward signal, objective, loss, advantage calculation, negative examples, filtering criterion, or key hyperparameters. Without these details, it is difficult to reproduce or distinguish from supervised fine-tuning on successful trajectories.

Important experimental details are missing from the main text, including the number of runs, sampling parameters, Pass@1/Pass@4 protocol, API versions and dates, prompts, emulator or browser snapshots, random seeds, and failure cases caused by environmental nondeterminism.

The benchmark depends on live websites and applications such as IMDb, Wikipedia, and Douban. Although the conclusion briefly notes that real interfaces change, the paper does not explain how reproducibility will be preserved through fixed snapshots, versioned emulators, archived content, or continuous maintenance.

Human curation relies on two graduate researchers, but no annotation guidelines, adjudication procedure, or inter-annotator agreement is reported. This matters for the claim that the dataset is high quality.

The WPSR difficulty score is not fully specified: the paper states that it depends on pathway length and number of applications but does not give the exact function combining these factors. The implementation and sensitivity of this weighting should be validated.

The claims of generalization from the A3 experiment are somewhat overstated. The improvement from 26.3% to 36.8% success rate comes from one selected benchmark setting, reports only SR, and has no confidence intervals or significance testing.

The results lack statistical treatment. Repeated-run variance, bootstrap confidence intervals, or paired significance tests would be especially appropriate given stochastic API models and the relatively modest 276-task benchmark.

The error-analysis pies do not explain how errors were annotated, whether labels were manually or automatically derived, or how many trajectories contributed to each breakdown, so the reliability of the taxonomy is hard to judge.

The scale is moderate for a benchmark intended to represent diverse real-world workflows. More evidence is needed on coverage across application categories, interaction types, locales, and UI changes.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely problem: evaluating long-horizon GUI agents under realistic linguistic ambiguity while retaining deterministic verification.

The benchmark design has a promising conceptual core: decoupling structured Wikidata/RDF causal paths from their natural-language realizations, with controls for non-linear sequencing, noise, contextual parameters, and cross-app dependencies.

NaturalGAIA spans 276 tasks across 25 applications and three difficulty levels, and it includes a two-stage human solvability/consistency verification process plus freeze-frame handling for time-sensitive information.

The proposed LightManus-Jarvis decomposition is sensible: a macro planner manages topology and memory, while a micro executor uses hybrid screenshot/accessibility-tree perception and UID-based actions to reduce coordinate hallucination.

The empirical matrix is broad, covering several closed and open-source MLLMs, multiple baselines, planner/executor ablations, efficiency measurements, error analysis, and supplementary AndroidWorld/Mind2Web comparisons.

The controlled Gemini-2.5-Pro comparison in the main text—Mobile-Agent-e at 21.1%, LightManus-MAe at 28.3%, and LightManus-Jarvis at 38.3% WPSR—provides preliminary evidence that both the planner and executor contribute to performance.
weaknesses: The central realism and long-horizon claims are overstated. The benchmark contains only 276 tasks, with 51 advanced tasks and causal paths of only 1–7 atomic tasks (average 3.1); actual UI-action trajectory lengths are not reported. It also deliberately uses static, immutable information sources and excludes dynamic or irreversible scenarios.

The headline comparison is not fully controlled. The abstract reports 45.6% for the proposed system with a strong backend versus 21.1% for Mobile-Agent-e with Gemini-2.5-Pro, but no matched-backend baseline is reported for the system attaining 45.6%. The matched Gemini-2.5-Pro gain is 38.3% versus 21.1%.

The word “significantly” is used throughout without confidence intervals, statistical tests, variance estimates, or a clear number of independent runs. The Pass@1/Pass@4 sampling protocol and temperature settings are also insufficiently specified.

Reproducibility is inadequate for a benchmark paper. In the provided manuscript, the public-code link is blank, and the release does not clearly provide the task dataset, verifier implementation, environment snapshots, app versions, full prompts, model configurations, seeds, action budgets, or failure-handling rules.

Several evaluation metrics are under-specified. The difficulty score D is not formally operationalized, the positional weight p(i) in p-ATSR is merely described as monotonic, and WPSR’s instance/path weighting is difficult to reconstruct from the text.

MATCR counts only the number of consecutive successful atomic tasks from the beginning of a path. This measures prefix completion, not overall task completion or recovery after failure, so its name and interpretation may be misleading.

The claimed path-invariant verification is not fully reconciled with the strict dependency chains and expected intermediate atomic outputs. It remains unclear how tolerant the verifier is to alternative valid routes and how often text-match or state-match checks produce false positives or negatives.

Human validation lacks reliability evidence. The paper does not report the number of annotators, their qualifications, adjudication procedure, disagreement rates, inter-annotator agreement, human success rates, or time required to solve tasks.

The error taxonomy is inconsistent: Section 3.2 defines KD, PE, and OE, while Section 5.3 reports KD, PRE, OE, PE, and SCE. The annotation rules, boundaries between categories, and reliability of this attribution are not described.

Natural-language task generation relies on LLM templates, but the paper provides no quantitative analysis of linguistic diversity, ambiguity distribution, accidental entity leakage, template repetition, or contamination from model pretraining data.

Baseline fairness is hard to assess. The systems differ in environments, observation spaces, prompts, and accessibility information, and the adaptation/configuration of PC-Agent, Mobile-Agent-e, and UI-TARS is not documented in enough detail to isolate architectural gains from engineering advantages.

Efficiency results are potentially confounded. Token consumption depends heavily on prompt design and XML/screenshot compression, while wall-clock duration depends on network latency, emulator waits, app response time, and hardware. The efficiency evaluation also covers a narrow set of Level-3 conditions.

The context-evolution and global-memory mechanisms are described at a high level. Equation (5) indicates that prior feedback is inserted into the next task description, but the memory representation, update policy, retrieval scope, conflict resolution, and error-recovery behavior are not sufficiently specified to reimplement.

The supplementary AndroidWorld and Mind2Web results are encouraging but too briefly reported: task subsets, adaptation details, repeated runs, statistical uncertainty, and verifier behavior are not described thoroughly enough to support a broad generalizability claim.

Although the authors acknowledge some limitations, the current evidence does not yet establish NaturalGAIA as a high-fidelity real-world benchmark or the architecture’s superiority as a general result. Substantial benchmark validation, metric clarification, controlled experiments, and artifact release are needed before the paper is ready for Findings.
